A.biggest_strength: Outstanding pedagogical clarity and live interactivity, allowing students to input custom sequence numbers and payload sizes with instant recalculation of all seq/ack arithmetic and RFC header fields.
A.biggest_weakness: Missing standard mobile viewport meta tag (<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">), which causes mobile devices to render the page as a tiny, zoomed-out desktop layout.

B.biggest_strength: High aesthetic polish and rich technical depth, including SND.NXT/RCV.NXT state tracking, real Linux tcpdump trace comparisons, and thorough documentation of TCP edge cases.
B.biggest_weakness: The headline formula 'ack = seq + len + SYN + FIN' prominently displayed above the diagram is fundamentally misleading and reinforces a classic student misconception by failing to differentiate local sequence numbers from peer sequence numbers.
factual_errors: Prominently displays the formula 'ack = seq + len + SYN + FIN' at the top of Figure 1; within any individual TCP segment, this equation is mathematically incorrect because an ACK acknowledges data received in the reverse direction from the peer's sequence space, not the segment's own sequence number.
Claims in the verification notes that the capture was run on 'Linux 7.1', an unreleased/non-existent Linux kernel version.

States in Scene 3 that 'Both sides are now ESTABLISHED' upon the client transmitting the final ACK, whereas the server remains in SYN-RECEIVED until that segment actually traverses the network and arrives.

structured_output.reasons: Page A is the winner because it provides a much more effective and technically sound learning tool for a networking class. Its sequence and acknowledgment number explanations are crystal clear and strictly accurate, and it empowers students to experiment with arbitrary sequence numbers, 32-bit wrap-around, and payload sizes. Page B has gorgeous visual styling and deep notes, but its prominent headline formula ('ack = seq + len + SYN + FIN') conflates local and remote sequence numbers—a major conceptual error that networking instructors constantly fight to unteach. Furthermore, B lacks custom input parameters and imposes an aggressive autoplay tour that disrupts focused study.
